title: Wheated Bourbon Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What makes a bourbon wheated, how wheat changes the taste compared with rye and how to taste a wheated bourbon properly.
teaser: Take the rye out of bourbon and put wheat in. The result is softer, rounder and sweeter. Here is why.
standfirst: Most bourbons use rye as their second grain. A wheated bourbon uses wheat instead. That one swap changes the taste more than you might expect. This guide explains the style and how to taste it.
sections: The swap that defines the style

Bourbon must contain at least 51% corn. The rest of the mash bill is the distiller's choice. Most bourbons use rye as the flavouring grain and a little malted barley for its enzymes. A wheated bourbon replaces the rye with wheat.

A typical wheated mash bill might be around 70% corn, 15 to 20% wheat and the rest malted barley. Some use more wheat, some less. The rules are the same as any bourbon: made in the United States, distilled to no more than 80% ABV, filled at no more than 62.5% ABV into new charred oak and bottled at no less than 40% ABV.

Rye brings spice: pepper, clove, mint and rye bread. Wheat brings almost none of that. Instead it gives a softer, rounder texture and a gentle bready, honeyed sweetness. With the spice gone, the corn and the oak have more room. Vanilla, caramel and toffee from the new charred barrel come through more clearly.

People often describe wheated bourbons as smooth or easy. That can mean they are gentle, or that they are simply less spicy. Taste one next to a rye recipe to judge for yourself. Our guide to bourbon mash bills covers the rye recipes for comparison.

Wheat contains less of the compounds that give rye its spicy, grassy character. It ferments cleanly and gives a spirit that is lighter on spice and a touch sweeter. Distillers still make cuts and choose a distillation strength, so two wheated bourbons can taste quite different.

Wheat also brings its own handling quirks. It is high in protein and can make a sticky mash, though not usually as troublesome as rye. Distillers manage it with enzymes and careful cooking.

Every bourbon goes into new charred oak. The barrel gives much of the colour and flavour. The char creates a layer of charcoal that filters some harsh compounds. The toasted wood under it gives vanilla, caramel, coconut and spice. Without rye spice to compete, a wheated bourbon often shows these oak flavours more plainly.

That also means a wheated bourbon can taste woody if it spends too long in a hot warehouse. Age statements and tasting notes help, but your own palate is the best guide.

Bourbon matures in places with hot summers and cold winters. The wood breathes as the temperature swings. Indian heat pushes maturation even faster. If you ever taste whisky aged in India next to bourbon, notice how both take colour and oak quickly. Our guide to ex-bourbon, sherry and wine casks explains where used bourbon barrels go next, including into Indian and Scottish warehouses.
How to taste a wheated bourbon

• Pour about 15 ml into a tulip shaped glass. A tumbler lets too much aroma escape.
  • Nose it gently, mouth slightly open. Look for honey, bread, vanilla and caramel.
  • Take a small sip and hold it for a few seconds. Notice the texture: soft or sharp, thin or round.
  • Add a few drops of water. Many bourbons are bottled well above 40% ABV. Water opens the aroma.
  • Compare with a rye recipe bourbon in an identical glass. The difference in spice is the lesson.

Keep the measures small and drink water between them. Never drink and drive after tasting.

Few labels say wheated in large letters. Some distilleries publish the mash bill on their website or the back label. Others describe the whiskey as soft or smooth without saying why. If the grain matters to you, look up the producer before you buy.

Watch for other label terms too. Straight bourbon means at least two years in new charred oak with nothing added. Bottled in bond means at least four years old, from one distillation season at one distillery, bottled at 50% ABV. Cask strength or barrel proof means the whiskey was not reduced much, if at all, before bottling. A cask strength wheated bourbon can be well over 55% ABV, so add water and go slowly. Our guide to straight bourbon and bottled in bond explains those terms.

The softer, sweeter profile works well with desserts that have caramel or nut flavours. In India, try it with a small piece of chikki or a caramel custard. With savoury food, the sweetness sits well next to smoky grilled meats or a tandoori platter. These are suggestions, not rules. Trust what your own palate tells you.

Next time you buy bourbon, check whether the distillery publishes its mash bill. If it is wheated, taste it next to a rye recipe you already know and write one sentence on each. That one comparison will teach you to recognise wheat in a blind tasting.
faqs: A bourbon that uses wheat instead of rye as its secondary grain, alongside at least 51% corn and some malted barley.
It often tastes softer and sweeter because there is no rye spice. The corn sweetness and oak flavours come through more clearly.
Yes. It follows all the bourbon rules: made in the US, at least 51% corn, new charred oak and bottled at no less than 40% ABV.
What glass is best for tasting bourbon?
A tulip shaped glass concentrates the aroma better than a wide tumbler, making it easier to pick out notes.
